a: Exonumia is the study and collection of items that function as money or resemble money but are not official legal tender, including tokens, medals, badges, counterstamped coins, elongated coins, and other coin-like objects that offer insight into commerce, military tradition, and commemorative culture. Challenge coins are small medallions bearing an organization's emblem, originating from a World War I tradition where a wealthy lieutenant had bronze medallions struck for his squadron—one pilot later used his coin to prove his identity when captured by French forces, establishing the tradition of carrying unit coins. The challenge coin custom typically works as follows: a person challenges others by slapping their coin on a bar or table, and everyone challenged must produce their coin immediately—those who fail must buy a round of drinks, while the challenger buys if everyone shows their coin, with strict rules about the coin never being attached to a belt or carried in a way that makes it immediately visible, and variations including presidential coins (given by the President to service members), unit coins, memorial coins, and commemorative issue coins from all branches of the military.

US military medals decorations order of precedence

a: US military medals are worn in order of precedence, with the Medal of Honor (the nation's highest military decoration, awarded for conspicuous gallantry above and beyond the call of duty) at the top, followed by Service Crosses (Distinguished Service Cross, Navy Cross, Air Force Cross, Coast Guard Cross), Distinguished Service Medals, Silver Star, Legion of Merit, Distinguished Flying Cross, Bronze Star, and Purple Heart. Campaign and service medals include specific awards for participation in named conflicts, and civilian awards such as the Presidential Medal of Freedom (the highest civilian honor) and the Congressional Gold Medal recognize exceptional contributions to national security, world peace, or cultural achievement. UK gallantry medals follow a different system, with the Victoria Cross (the highest British award for valor, made from the bronze of captured Russian guns) and the George Cross (for civilian gallantry) at the apex, followed by the Distinguished Service Order, the Conspicuous Gallantry Cross, and a hierarchy of Distinguished Service Cross, Military Cross, Distinguished Flying Cross, and Mention in Despatches, while campaign stars from WWII include the 1939-45 Star, Atlantic Star, Africa Star, Pacific Star, and others, collectively known as the WWII campaign stars, worn with the Defence Medal and War Medal.

types of tokens collectible exonumia

a: Tokens are coin-like objects issued by private entities for specific purposes: trade tokens and store cards were used by merchants, especially in the 19th century, as advertising and as small change during coin shortages, while transportation tokens (bridge, subway, bus, ferry, and turnpike tokens) were issued by transit authorities worldwide before electronic fare systems. Casino tokens and gaming chips include poker chips used in card rooms, slot machine tokens used before ticket-in-ticket-out systems, and commemorative chips issued for special events, with high-end casino chips made of clay composite in distinctive colors and edge markings for security. Hobo nickels are Buffalo nickels carved or engraved by itinerant workers during the Great Depression, transforming the Indian head into caricatures, portraits, or animals, while love tokens are coins that have been smoothed on one or both sides and engraved with initials, names, dates, or decorative designs, originally given as sentimental keepsakes. Encased coins are coins inserted into a metal or plastic frame that displays an advertisement or message, and elongated coins (pressed pennies) are created by rolling a penny through a pair of engraved rollers that emboss a design onto the elongated metal.

medal manufacturing techniques finishes
striking proof-like relief alignment edge types mint marks
a: Medals and exonumia are manufactured using dies and planchets under high pressure striking, with variations in finish including proof (polished dies and planchets producing mirror fields and frosted devices), brilliant uncirculated (standard minting quality with original luster but no special polishing), matte proof (a sandblasted appearance), reverse proof (frosted fields with mirrored devices), and antique finish (artificially darkened to highlight relief details). Relief height ranges from standard to high relief and ultra high relief, which require multiple strikes to fully bring up the design and produce more dramatic sculptural quality. Coin alignment means the reverse is oriented upside-down when the obverse is right-side up (used for most circulating coins), while medal alignment means the reverse is right-side up when the obverse is right-side up (used for medals and some commemorative coins). Edge finishes can be plain, reeded, lettered, or ornamental, with edge lettering, edge numbering, and edge inscription providing additional security features, while mint marks (indicating the mint facility) and privy marks (special symbols added for commemorative issues or as anti-counterfeiting features) are important identifying details, along with designer initials and engraver signatures that credit the artists who created the design.
